Provider-initiated testing and counselling normalises HIV testing in clinical settings.
Pre-test counselling explains the purpose of the HIV test and what the results mean.
Post-test counselling provides support and guidance regardless of the HIV test result.
A reactive HIV rapid test must be confirmed with a second different rapid test.
HIV self-test kits are available at pharmacies and some clinics.
A positive HIV self-test result must always be confirmed at a health facility.
HIV testing during pregnancy is offered at the first antenatal visit.
Repeat HIV testing in the third trimester is recommended for HIV-negative pregnant women.
Index case testing offers HIV tests to sexual partners and children of newly diagnosed people.
Social network testing reaches people who would not otherwise test for HIV.
Mobile HIV testing units bring testing services to communities and workplaces.
HIV testing campaigns during public events increase testing uptake.
Knowing your HIV status is the first step to protecting yourself and others.
HIV testing is confidential and your results will not be shared without your consent.
Disclosing your HIV status to a trusted person can reduce isolation and improve wellbeing.
HIV disclosure to a sexual partner is important to prevent transmission.
Disclosure counselling helps people decide when, how, and to whom to disclose their HIV status.
Children living with HIV should be told their status in an age-appropriate way.
Disclosure of HIV status to children should be done gradually and with professional support.
Fear of rejection and violence can make HIV disclosure very difficult.
Healthcare providers should support patients through the disclosure process.
Assisted disclosure involves a healthcare worker helping a patient tell their partner about their HIV status.
People should never be forced to disclose their HIV status against their will.
Workplace disclosure of HIV status is a personal decision and cannot be required by an employer.
Adolescents living with HIV face unique challenges including stigma, disclosure, and transition to adult care.
Transition from paediatric to adult HIV care is a critical period that requires careful planning.
Adolescents should be involved in decisions about their HIV care.
Youth-friendly HIV services are designed to meet the specific needs of adolescents.
Peer support groups for HIV-positive adolescents improve adherence and mental health.
School-based HIV education programmes reduce risky behaviour in adolescents.
Comprehensive sexuality education includes HIV prevention as a core component.
Adolescents have the right to access HIV testing and treatment without parental consent in many countries.
HIV-positive adolescents who are virally suppressed can live full and healthy lives.
Substance use among adolescents increases HIV risk and should be addressed in prevention programmes.
Older adults are often overlooked in HIV prevention and testing programmes.
HIV in older adults is frequently diagnosed late because clinicians do not consider it.
Older adults living with HIV have higher rates of depression and social isolation.
Cognitive decline is more common in older people living with HIV.
ART dosing may need to be adjusted in older adults with kidney or liver impairment.
Older adults living with HIV should be screened for frailty at every clinic visit.
Comprehensive geriatric assessment is increasingly relevant for older people living with HIV.
Retirement and bereavement can trigger depression in older people living with HIV.
Sexual health remains important for older adults living with HIV.
Older adults should be included in HIV clinical trials to ensure treatments are appropriate for them.
HIV stigma is a violation of human rights and a barrier to ending the HIV epidemic.
Contact-based education where people living with HIV share their stories reduces stigma.
Healthcare worker stigma towards people living with HIV must be actively addressed.
Stigma reduction training for healthcare workers improves quality of HIV care.
Self-stigma occurs when a person internalises negative beliefs about their HIV status.
Community-level stigma reduction programmes create supportive environments for people living with HIV.
Media campaigns that show people living with HIV as healthy and productive reduce stigma.
Language matters in HIV — avoid terms like AIDS victim or HIV sufferer.
Use people-first language such as person living with HIV rather than HIV patient.
Stigma and discrimination against people living with HIV are illegal in many countries.
HIV-positive women have the same right to choose whether to have children as HIV-negative women.
Contraceptive counselling should be offered to all HIV-positive women of reproductive age.
Dual protection using condoms and contraception prevents both HIV transmission and unintended pregnancy.
Hormonal contraception does not increase the risk of HIV acquisition.
Intrauterine devices are safe and effective for HIV-positive women.
Cervical cancer screening should be done annually for HIV-positive women.
HPV vaccination is recommended for HIV-positive girls and young women.
HIV-positive women have a higher risk of cervical cancer due to immune suppression.
Menopause may occur earlier in women living with HIV.
Hormone replacement therapy for menopause is generally safe for HIV-positive women on ART.
People living with HIV have a higher risk of certain cancers including Kaposi sarcoma and lymphoma.
Kaposi sarcoma is caused by human herpesvirus 8 and is more common in people with low CD4 counts.
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is an AIDS-defining cancer that occurs at low CD4 counts.
ART reduces the risk of AIDS-defining cancers by restoring immune function.
Chronic pain is common in people living with HIV and requires assessment and management.
Peripheral neuropathy causes burning and tingling in the feet and is common in people living with HIV.
HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder affects memory, concentration, and daily functioning.
Sleep disturbances are more common in people living with HIV and affect quality of life.
Fatigue is one of the most commonly reported symptoms in people living with HIV.
Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for more than two thirds of all people living with HIV globally.
Eastern and southern Africa has the highest HIV burden of any region in the world.
South Africa has the largest HIV epidemic in the world with over seven million people living with HIV.
HIV incidence has declined significantly in sub-Saharan Africa over the past two decades.
AIDS-related deaths have declined by more than 60 percent since the peak in 2004.
The UNAIDS 95-95-95 targets aim to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.
The first 95 means 95 percent of people living with HIV know their status.
The second 95 means 95 percent of people who know their status are on ART.
The third 95 means 95 percent of people on ART are virally suppressed.
Achieving the 95-95-95 targets would prevent millions of new HIV infections and deaths.
HIV does not affect a person's ability to work in most occupations.
Employers should provide HIV education and testing programmes for their workforce.
Employee assistance programmes can support workers living with HIV.
HIV-positive employees are entitled to reasonable accommodation in the workplace.
Sick leave and flexible working arrangements support HIV-positive employees.
Workplace HIV policies should be developed in consultation with employees and unions.
Mining, transport, and agricultural sectors have high HIV prevalence in sub-Saharan Africa.
Long-distance truck drivers are a key population for HIV prevention interventions.
Migrant workers face increased HIV risk due to separation from families and social networks.
HIV programmes in the workplace reduce absenteeism and improve productivity.

You have the right to ask questions about your treatment at any time.
HIV is a manageable chronic condition and not a death sentence.
With proper treatment people living with HIV can have a near-normal life expectancy.
Early diagnosis and treatment are the most important factors in HIV outcomes.
HIV treatment is free at public health facilities in South Africa.
You do not need to pay for HIV medicine at a government clinic in South Africa.
HIV is not transmitted through sharing food, utensils, toilets, or swimming pools.
You cannot get HIV from hugging, shaking hands, or casual contact with an HIV-positive person.
Mosquitoes and other insects cannot transmit HIV.
HIV is not transmitted through saliva, tears, or sweat.
Understanding how HIV is and is not transmitted helps reduce fear and stigma.
HIV can be transmitted from a mother to her baby through breastfeeding if the mother is not on ART.
Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) reduces the risk of HIV infection in HIV-negative individuals.
Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) must be started within 72 hours of a potential HIV exposure.
Voluntary medical male circumcision reduces the risk of female-to-male HIV transmission by up to 60%.
HIV is not transmitted by sharing food, utensils, or toilet seats.
Consistent condom use during every sexual encounter significantly reduces HIV transmission risk.
Harm reduction strategies such as needle exchange programmes reduce HIV risk among people who inject drugs.
Sexual violence survivors should access PEP services as soon as possible after an assault.
HIV-positive individuals on effective ART with an undetectable viral load cannot sexually transmit the virus.
The U=U message — Undetectable equals Untransmittable — is a powerful tool against HIV stigma.
HIV self-testing kits allow people to test privately at home and receive results within minutes.
Community-based HIV testing reaches populations who do not access facility-based services.
HIV testing during antenatal care is a critical entry point for PMTCT programmes.
Index testing involves offering HIV tests to sexual partners and biological children of a known HIV-positive person.
A negative HIV test result does not rule out recent infection if the test is taken during the window period.
Dolutegravir-based regimens are now the preferred first-line ART in most national guidelines.
Patients who experience side effects from ART should consult their healthcare provider before stopping treatment.
Drug resistance testing helps clinicians select the most effective ART regimen for each patient.
Long-acting injectable ART formulations are an emerging option for patients who struggle with daily oral dosing.
Switching ART regimens should be guided by viral load results and clinical assessment.
Patients on ART should have their kidney and liver function monitored regularly.
Lipid profiles should be monitored in patients on certain ART regimens due to cardiovascular risk.
Bone mineral density can decrease in some patients on long-term ART; calcium and vitamin D supplementation may help.
ART reduces HIV-related inflammation that contributes to non-AIDS comorbidities.
Patients should bring all their medications to every clinic visit to support medication reconciliation.
Cryptococcal meningitis is a life-threatening fungal infection common in people with advanced HIV disease.
Fluconazole prophylaxis is recommended for HIV-positive patients with low CD4 counts to prevent cryptococcal disease.
Toxoplasma encephalitis can occur in HIV-positive patients with CD4 counts below 100 cells/mm³.
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis can cause blindness in people with advanced HIV and requires urgent treatment.
Kaposi sarcoma is an AIDS-defining cancer caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8).
Anxiety and depression are significantly more common among people living with HIV than in the general population.
Integrating mental health services into HIV care improves both treatment adherence and quality of life.
Cognitive impairment associated with HIV can affect memory, concentration, and daily functioning.
Substance use disorders increase HIV risk behaviours and complicate treatment adherence.
Trauma-informed care approaches are essential when supporting HIV-positive survivors of gender-based violence.
Sex workers face elevated HIV risk due to multiple partners, limited negotiating power, and criminalisation.
Decriminalisation of same-sex relationships and sex work is associated with better HIV outcomes.
Transgender women have a disproportionately high burden of HIV globally.
Migrants and refugees may face legal and language barriers to accessing HIV testing and treatment.
Incarcerated individuals have higher HIV prevalence and require access to prevention and treatment services in prisons.
Adequate protein intake supports immune function and helps maintain muscle mass in people living with HIV.
Micronutrient deficiencies, particularly zinc and selenium, are common in people living with HIV.
Smoking cessation is strongly recommended for people living with HIV due to elevated cardiovascular and lung cancer risk.
Regular physical activity improves physical and mental health outcomes in people living with HIV.
Alcohol use can reduce ART adherence and accelerate liver disease in people living with HIV.
